:::: {.vcenter}
::: {.statement}
A parameter set is not a result.
:::

::: {.statement-hi}
A result is a parameter set<br>plus a statement of where it may be used.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Say this before any equation appears, and say it again at the end. Module 1 was
about which physics a model contains. This module is about what evidence a
number rests on. The two halves of the course meet here: the equation of state
told us how a fluid behaves, and now we ask how we know.

**ASK THE CLASS**
You have a fitted NRTL parameter pair from a paper. What would you need to know
before using it in a column simulation?

## What this module establishes

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Introduction
:::

::: {.lede}
Four descriptions of the same equilibrium, then the full working cycle: data,
consistency, regression, and a stated domain of validity.
:::

:::::: {.columns}
::::: {.column width="48%"}
:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[The chain of reasoning]{.card-h .c-teal}

An equation of state gives $P$-$V$-$T$ behaviour → equilibrium is governed by
chemical potential → fugacity gives chemical potential a usable form → equality
of fugacity predicts phase equilibrium.

Module 4 is where that chain meets measurement.

:::
::::
:::::

::::: {.column width="48%"}
:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[Five questions]{.card-h .c-amber}

- Which description of VLE, and what does it cost?
- What is actually measured, and how well?
- Can this dataset be believed?
- Which model, fitted against what?
- Where may the answer be used?

:::
::::
:::::
::::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Put the five questions on the board and leave them there for the whole module.
Every slide answers one of them; students should be able to say which.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That this module is about learning NRTL. NRTL takes ten minutes. The module is
about evidence, and the model is the smallest part of it.
:::

## Four descriptions of one equilibrium {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
PART I
:::

::: {.lede}
Section 4.1&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Raoult, modified Raoult, gamma-phi, phi-phi<br>Each rung adds physics the rung below omitted, and each addition costs something.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Draw the deliberate parallel with the equation-of-state ladder from Module 1.
The visual rhyme is not decoration: it is the same argument applied to a
different question, and students who saw it once will see it faster the second
time.
:::

## Raoult's law, and its two assumptions

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.1 · Four descriptions of the same equilibrium
:::

::: {.lede}
State the two assumptions separately, because they fail separately.
:::

$$y_i P = x_i P_i^{\rm sat}$$

:::::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card}

[Assumption 1 — ideal liquid]{.card-h .c-teal}

Every molecule sees the same environment whatever the composition. True only
when the two species are chemically almost identical: benzene and toluene,
hexane and heptane.

:::

::: {.card}

[Assumption 2 — ideal vapour]{.card-h .c-amber}

$\hat\varphi_i = 1$. Fails at high pressure, and also at low pressure when the
vapour associates. Acetic acid dimerises in the vapour at one atmosphere.

:::

::: {.card}

[What it costs]{.card-h .c-rust}

Nothing but $P_i^{\rm sat}(T)$. No binary parameter, no data, no fitting.
That is why it survives as the first estimate.

:::
::::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Insist on the separation. Students learn "Raoult's law assumes ideality" as one
sentence and then cannot diagnose which half failed when it does.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That the vapour assumption is safe below one atmosphere. Acetic acid is the
counterexample that kills it: association is a chemical effect, not a pressure
effect. The dataset for this is in the course paper library.

**ASK THE CLASS**
Name a pair for which assumption 1 holds and assumption 2 fails. Then the
reverse.
:::

## Modified Raoult's law

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.1 · Four descriptions of the same equilibrium
:::

::: {.lede}
Liquid non-ideality admitted; the vapour still treated as an ideal gas.
:::

$$y_i P = x_i \gamma_i P_i^{\rm sat}$$

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[Physical meaning]{.card-h .c-amber}

$\gamma_i$ measures how much the liquid environment differs from the pure
liquid. It is a property of the *mixture*, derived from an excess Gibbs energy,
and it carries the reference state with it — Lewis-Randall here, so
$\gamma_i \to 1$ as $x_i \to 1$.

:::

::: {.card}

[Engineering implication]{.card-h .c-teal}

This is the description behind almost every distillation column ever designed
at moderate pressure. Two fitted parameters per binary pair, from binary VLE
data. Everything in Sections 4.2 to 4.4 is about where those two numbers come
from and what they are worth.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Emphasise that $\gamma$ is not a fudge factor. It is defined, it obeys
Gibbs-Duhem, and that constraint is what makes the whole of Section 4.3
possible.

**ASK THE CLASS**
If $\gamma_1 > 1$, is the mixture easier or harder to separate than an ideal
one? Under what circumstance does that reverse?
:::

## The gamma-phi formulation

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.1 · Four descriptions of the same equilibrium
:::

::: {.lede}
Both phases non-ideal — but described by two different kinds of model.
:::

$$y_i \hat\varphi_i P
  = x_i \gamma_i P_i^{\rm sat} \varphi_i^{\rm sat}
    \exp\!\left[\frac{v_i^L\,(P - P_i^{\rm sat})}{RT}\right]$$

:::::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card}

[$\hat\varphi_i$]{.card-h .c-teal}

Vapour fugacity coefficient, from an equation of state. The two-term virial
equation is enough below a few bar.

:::

::: {.card}

[$\varphi_i^{\rm sat}$]{.card-h .c-amber}

The same quantity for the pure saturated vapour. It is the reference the liquid
fugacity is measured against, and it does not cancel.

:::

::: {.card}

[Poynting factor]{.card-h .c-rust}

Corrects the liquid from $P_i^{\rm sat}$ to $P$. Small below a few bar, but it
is not zero, and omitting it silently is not the same as knowing it is small.

:::
::::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Write the three correction factors as one group $\Phi_i$ and show that setting
$\Phi_i = 1$ returns the previous slide exactly. Students should see that these
descriptions are nested, not alternative.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That $\varphi_i^{\rm sat}$ cancels against $\hat\varphi_i$. It does not, except
for a pure component.
:::

## The phi-phi formulation

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.1 · Four descriptions of the same equilibrium
:::

::: {.lede}
One equation of state for both phases. The only option above the critical
temperature of a component.
:::

$$y_i \hat\varphi_i^{\,V} = x_i \hat\varphi_i^{\,L}$$

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[Why it is needed]{.card-h .c-amber}

A supercritical component has no $P_i^{\rm sat}$, so the whole right-hand side
of the gamma-phi equation is undefined. Natural gas, hydrogen, supercritical
CO₂: there is no vapour pressure to refer to.

:::

::: {.card}

[What it costs]{.card-h .c-rust}

One equation of state that must describe a dense liquid and a dilute vapour
with the same parameters, a binary interaction parameter $k_{ij}$ fitted to
data, and a root selection problem — the cubic has three roots and choosing
wrongly gives a confidently wrong answer.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Connect back to Module 1: this is why the cubics were worth all that trouble.
The reward for one equation that spans both phases is a description of
equilibrium that survives the critical point.

**ASK THE CLASS**
Why can a gamma-phi calculation not be pushed to the mixture critical point,
even with a very good activity model?
:::

## The ladder

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.1 · Four descriptions of the same equilibrium
:::

::: {.lede}
Each rung is exact given its own assumptions. Choosing a rung is choosing which
assumption to defend.
:::

![](figures/f4_01_vle_ladder.png){.fig-xl}

::: {.source}
F4.1 · The four descriptions, with the physics added and the cost incurred at each step.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Walk up from the bottom naming only the physics added, not the equations. The
vertical axis is physical content, not accuracy and not calendar time.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That higher is better. A phi-phi calculation on an ethanol/water column at one
atmosphere is slower, needs more parameters, and is *worse* than modified
Raoult with a decent activity model. Content is only worth its cost when your
problem contains that physics.

**ASK THE CLASS**
Which rung for: an ethanol/water column at 1 atm; a natural gas separator at
80 bar; an acetic acid/water column at 1 atm? The third is the interesting one.
:::

## Choosing a description

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.1 · Four descriptions of the same equilibrium
:::

::: {.lede}
A decision table, not a ranking.
:::

| System | Description | Because |
|---|---|---|
| Benzene / toluene, 1 atm | Raoult | Chemically similar; no binary data needed |
| Ethanol / water, 1 atm | Modified Raoult | Strongly non-ideal liquid, near-ideal vapour |
| Acetic acid / water, 1 atm | Gamma-phi | Vapour associates; $\hat\varphi \ne 1$ at 1 atm |
| Methane / propane, 80 bar | Phi-phi | One component is supercritical |
| CO₂ / ethanol, 100 bar | Phi-phi with a $G^E$ mixing rule | Supercritical *and* polar — see the appendix |

::: {.note}
The last row is the case neither classical description handles, and it is why
the appendix to this deck exists.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Make the students defend one row each. The acetic acid row is the one that
teaches the most, because the pressure is low and the naive answer is wrong.

**ASK THE CLASS**
Which row would change if the column ran at 10 bar instead of 1?
:::

## From measurement to activity coefficient {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
PART II
:::

::: {.lede}
Section 4.2&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A reported $\gamma$ is not a measurement.<br>It is four measured numbers and two assumptions.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
This is the shortest section and the one students most often skip. Slow down.
Everything in Sections 4.3 and 4.4 inherits the errors introduced here.
:::

## What a VLE apparatus measures

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.2 · From measurement to activity coefficient
:::

::: {.lede}
Four numbers per point, each with its own uncertainty, and none of them is
$\gamma$.
:::

:::::: {.cards .quad}
::: {.card}

[Temperature]{.card-h .c-teal}

Calibrated thermometer in the boiling liquid. Typically $\pm 0.05$ K.
Its error enters through $P_i^{\rm sat}(T)$, which is exponential in $T$.

:::

::: {.card}

[Pressure]{.card-h .c-amber}

Manometer or transducer. Typically $\pm 0.05$ kPa. Usually the *best* measured
variable, which is why Barker's method uses it.

:::

::: {.card}

[Liquid composition]{.card-h .c-rust}

Sample and analyse — refractometry, gas chromatography, density. Typically
$\pm 0.001$ mole fraction, and only if the calibration is honest.

:::

::: {.card}

[Vapour composition]{.card-h .c-sky}

Condense and analyse. The hardest measurement: partial condensation, holdup,
and entrainment all bias it. Typically $\pm 0.002$, often worse.

:::
::::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Ask which of the four would you drop if you could only measure three. The
answer — $y$ — is exactly what Barker's method does, and it prepares Section
4.4.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That an old dataset is worse than a modern one because the instruments were
cruder. Often the reverse: careful 1950s recirculating-still work with
gravimetric analysis beats a hurried modern GC calibration.
:::

## Computing gamma

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.2 · From measurement to activity coefficient
:::

::: {.lede}
Two assumptions convert four measurements into an activity coefficient.
:::

$$\gamma_i = \frac{y_i \Phi_i P}{x_i P_i^{\rm sat}(T)},
\qquad
\Phi_i = \frac{\hat\varphi_i}{\varphi_i^{\rm sat}}
\exp\!\left[-\frac{v_i^L (P - P_i^{\rm sat})}{RT}\right]$$

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[Assumption A — the vapour]{.card-h .c-amber}

Setting $\Phi_i = 1$ is modified Raoult. For acetone/chloroform at 50 °C the
virial correction shifts $\ln\gamma_1$ by up to 0.008 — small, but
**systematic**, and a consistency test reacts to systematic errors, not to
scatter.

:::

::: {.card}

[Assumption B — the vapour pressure]{.card-h .c-teal}

$P_i^{\rm sat}$ comes from a correlation, not from this experiment. Antoine
coefficients are copied between references with unit errors more often than any
other quantity in this subject. Check the correlation against the normal
boiling point before you trust one activity coefficient.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Do the boiling-point check live. It takes one line of code and it has caught a
wrong-isomer Antoine set in this course twice.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That the vapour correction is negligible because the pressure is low. Its size
is not the point — its *systematic* character is. A 0.008 bias in $\ln\gamma$
is invisible in a plot and fatal in a consistency test.
:::

## Where the error actually comes from

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.2 · From measurement to activity coefficient
:::

::: {.lede}
Propagate, and the ranking is not the one students expect.
:::

$$\sigma^2(\ln\gamma_1)
 = \left(\frac{\sigma_y}{y_1}\right)^{\!2}
 + \left(\frac{\sigma_P}{P}\right)^{\!2}
 + \left(\frac{\sigma_x}{x_1}\right)^{\!2}
 + \left(\frac{{\rm d}\ln P_1^{\rm sat}}{{\rm d}T}\,\sigma_T\right)^{\!2}$$

:::::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card}

[The temperature term]{.card-h .c-rust}

$P^{\rm sat}$ is exponential in $T$, so ${\rm d}\ln P^{\rm sat}/{\rm d}T$ is of
order $0.03\ {\rm K^{-1}}$ near the normal boiling point. A 0.05 K error is
then worth 0.0015 in $\ln\gamma$ — comparable to the composition term.

:::

::: {.card}

[The dilute ends]{.card-h .c-amber}

$\sigma_x/x_1$ blows up as $x_1 \to 0$. At $x_1 = 0.02$ a 0.001 error in
composition is 5 % in $\gamma_1$. That is exactly where the model is least
constrained and where $\gamma^\infty$ is read off.

:::

::: {.card}

[The consequence]{.card-h .c-teal}

Quoting $\gamma$ to four figures from a thermometer read to 0.1 K is
arithmetic, not measurement. Report the uncertainty or do not report the
figure.

:::
::::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Have them change one $\sigma$ at a time in the notebook and watch the ranking
change with composition. The instrument you should improve is not the same at
$x_1 = 0.05$ and $x_1 = 0.5$.

**ASK THE CLASS**
You have money for one better instrument. Which, and does your answer depend on
the composition range you care about?
:::

## Isothermal, isobaric, and the azeotrope

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.2 · From measurement to activity coefficient
:::

::: {.lede}
The two kinds of dataset, and the one composition where $\gamma$ comes for free.
:::

![](figures/f4_02_pxy_txy_azeotrope.png){.fig-cap width="78%"}

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[Isothermal is easier to use]{.card-h .c-teal}

At constant $T$ the Gibbs-Duhem equation has no enthalpy term. Isobaric data
are more common — that is how a column runs — and harder, because $T$ varies
across the composition range.

:::

::: {.card}

[The azeotrope is a free measurement]{.card-h .c-amber}

At $x_i = y_i$ the equilibrium condition gives
$\gamma_1 / \gamma_2 = P_2^{\rm sat} / P_1^{\rm sat}$ directly, with no vapour
sample at all. In an old dataset it is often the only point that can be
trusted without qualification.

:::
::::

::: {.source}
F4.2 · The same system as $P$-$x$-$y$ and as $T$-$x$-$y$, with the azeotrope marked on both.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Point out that the azeotrope is a maximum in $P$ on the left and a *minimum* in
$T$ on the right. Students confuse the two constantly, and the pair of panels
settles it.

**ASK THE CLASS**
Why does a maximum-pressure azeotrope appear as a minimum-boiling one?
:::

## Thermodynamic consistency {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
PART III
:::

::: {.lede}
Section 4.3&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Can this dataset be believed?<br>Gibbs-Duhem makes a binary VLE dataset over-determined, so the data can be tested against thermodynamics with no model assumed correct.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
This is the heart of the module and the part that transfers to every other
subject they will meet. The idea — use a physical constraint to test data
rather than to fit them — is general.
:::

## The premise

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.3 · Thermodynamic consistency testing
:::

::: {.lede}
One of the four measured variables is redundant. The size of the prediction
error is the test.
:::

$$x_1 \frac{{\rm d}\ln\gamma_1}{{\rm d}x_1}
 + x_2 \frac{{\rm d}\ln\gamma_2}{{\rm d}x_1} = 0
\qquad \text{(constant } T,\,P)$$

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[Satisfied by construction]{.card-h .c-teal}

Any model derived from a single $G^E$ satisfies this **identically** — the
residual is zero to machine precision. Finding otherwise means the code is
wrong, not the fluid.

:::

::: {.card}

[Satisfied by measurement]{.card-h .c-rust}

Data satisfy it only to within their errors. The two statements look alike on a
slide and are completely different in practice. Everything that follows is a
way of deciding whether the gap is noise or a real error.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Run both residuals in front of them. The model's is $10^{-11}$; the data's is
$10^{-2}$. The contrast is the whole section in one line of output.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That the test checks whether the data are *correct*. It checks whether they are
internally consistent with thermodynamics. A dataset can be consistent and
wrong — for instance if the sample was impure but the impurity behaved
smoothly.
:::

## The area test

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.3 · Thermodynamic consistency testing
:::

::: {.lede}
The oldest test, the most quoted, and the weakest.
:::

$$\int_0^1 \ln\frac{\gamma_1}{\gamma_2}\,{\rm d}x_1 = 0,
\qquad
D = 100\,\frac{|A^+ - A^-|}{A^+ + A^-}$$

![](figures/f4_03_area_test.png){.fig-lg width="60%"}

::: {.source}
F4.3 · The two areas whose difference must vanish, with $D$ reported.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Derive the integral in one line from Gibbs-Duhem so they see it is not a
recipe. Then say immediately that it is an integral, and integrals lose
information.

**ASK THE CLASS**
Before the next slide: what kind of error would this test fail to notice?
:::

## Why the area test is weak

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.3 · Thermodynamic consistency testing
:::

::: {.lede}
An integral cannot see an error that changes sign. This is a structural
limitation, not a matter of threshold.
:::

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[The construction]{.card-h .c-rust}

Perturbing $y_1$ shifts the measured ratio by
$\delta\ln(\gamma_1/\gamma_2) = \delta y_1 / [\,y_1(1-y_1)\,]$.

Choose $\delta y_1 = \varepsilon\, y_1 (1-y_1)(2x_1 - 1)$ and the ratio shifts
by $\varepsilon(2x_1-1)$ — odd about $x_1 = \tfrac12$, so it contributes
**exactly nothing** to the integral.

:::

::: {.card}

[The result]{.card-h .c-amber}

At $\varepsilon = 0.4$ the dataset is grossly wrong. The area test reports
$D = 1.3$ against a threshold of 10 — healthier than the merely noisy control —
while the point and direct tests both return the worst possible index.

An area test is a necessary condition. It is never a sufficient one.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Build the error live in the notebook rather than asserting it. Students who
have seen a dataset constructed to defeat a test stop treating a passed test as
a certificate.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That the fix is a tighter threshold. It is not. No threshold on an integral can
detect a function that integrates to zero.

**ASK THE CLASS**
Which Redlich-Kister coefficients of $\ln(\gamma_1/\gamma_2)$ can the area test
respond to at all?
:::

## The point test

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.3 · Thermodynamic consistency testing
:::

::: {.lede}
Van Ness, Byer and Gibbs: fit $P$-$x$ only, then predict $y$. Errors cannot
cancel, because nothing is integrated.
:::

![](figures/f4_04_point_test_residuals.png){.fig-cap width="62%"}

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[The logic]{.card-h .c-teal}

Barker's method uses only $P$ and $x$. If the data obey Gibbs-Duhem, $y$ is
already implied by the $P$-$x$ curve, so the fit must reproduce it. Mean
$|\delta y_1| < 0.01$ is the conventional pass.

:::

::: {.card}

[The trap]{.card-h .c-rust}

A large residual in $P$ means the **model** failed, not the data. Check
${\rm rms}\,\delta P$ before blaming the measurement, and use a model flexible
enough to follow the $P$-$x$ curve.

:::
::::

::: {.source}
F4.4 · Point-test residuals for a consistent and an inconsistent dataset on common axes.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Stress that this is local, not global. Every point contributes its own
residual, so an error of one sign in one half and the other sign in the other
half shows up twice rather than cancelling.

**ASK THE CLASS**
The residual is all of one sign and roughly constant. Now it changes sign once,
near the azeotrope. What causes each?
:::

## The direct test, and the 1-10 index

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.3 · Thermodynamic consistency testing
:::

::: {.lede}
The same redundancy, expressed in the variable Gibbs-Duhem is actually written
in. This is what modern journals expect.
:::

$$\delta = \ln\!\left(\frac{\gamma_1}{\gamma_2}\right)_{\!\rm exp}
        - \ln\!\left(\frac{\gamma_1}{\gamma_2}\right)_{\!\rm fitted}$$

| Index | RMS $\delta$ | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| 1 – 3 | < 0.075 | Good. Publishable without comment |
| 4 – 5 | 0.075 – 0.125 | Marginal. Requires an explanation |
| 6 – 10 | > 0.125 | Reject, or diagnose the fault |

::: {.note}
The fitted values come from a Barker fit to $P$-$x$ alone, so $\delta$ measures
the data, not the fit — provided the model follows $P$-$x$.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Point out that the index is a convention, not a probability. It is useful
because everyone uses the same one, and for no deeper reason.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That an index of 1 proves the data are right. It proves they are consistent
with thermodynamics under the vapour-phase assumption used to reduce them.
:::

## Two more tests, and what they add

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.3 · Thermodynamic consistency testing
:::

::: {.lede}
Different tests are blind to different things. That is the reason to run more
than one.
:::

:::::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card}

[Infinite dilution]{.card-h .c-teal}

Kojima's test compares $(G^E/RT)/x_1x_2$ with $\ln(\gamma_1/\gamma_2)$ at each
pure end point, where the two must coincide. Catches the dilute region, which
the area test averages away and where $\gamma^\infty$ is read off.

:::

::: {.card}

[Herington $D-J$]{.card-h .c-amber}

The area test with an empirical allowance $J = 150\,\Delta T/T_{\min}$ for the
temperature variation of an isobaric set. Widely required by referees; Wisniak
has shown it both passes bad data and fails good data.

:::

::: {.card}

[Wisniak L/W]{.card-h .c-rust}

Built on an energy balance rather than on $G^E$, so it responds to a different
combination of the measurements. Worth quoting when a dataset is contested.

:::
::::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Say plainly that Herington is a correlation, not a derivation, and that we
report it because reviewers ask for it. Students should know the difference
between a test with a derivation behind it and a test with a convention behind
it.
:::

## Isobaric data: the term that does not vanish

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.3 · Thermodynamic consistency testing
:::

::: {.lede}
At constant $P$ the temperature varies across the composition range, and the
excess enthalpy term returns.
:::

$$x_1 \frac{{\rm d}\ln\gamma_1}{{\rm d}x_1}
 + x_2 \frac{{\rm d}\ln\gamma_2}{{\rm d}x_1}
 = -\frac{H^E}{RT^2}\,\frac{{\rm d}T}{{\rm d}x_1}$$

![](figures/f4_09_excess_enthalpy_term.png){.fig-lg width="76%"}

::: {.source}
F4.9 · Size of the enthalpy term against the left-hand side, ethanol/water at 101.325 kPa. The $H^E$ magnitude is assumed and labelled as such on the figure.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
The honest teaching point is that we usually drop this term because we do not
have $H^E$, not because we have shown it is small. The figure shows when that
is defensible: in mid-range, yes; at the dilute ends, where ${\rm d}T/{\rm d}x$
is steep, no.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That isobaric data can be tested with the isothermal form and a shrug. They can
— everyone does — but the omission belongs in the report.
:::

## Three datasets, five tests

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.3 · Thermodynamic consistency testing
:::

![](figures/f4_05_three_datasets_tests.png){.fig-xl}

::: {.source}
F4.5 · The same experiment at three bias levels, with every statistic tabulated.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
The middle column is the one to dwell on. At $b = 0.06$ every test passes — the
area test by 0.3 of its threshold and the point test by 0.0005 — and the point
index is already 4. A dataset that passes on the third decimal place is not a
dataset that has been vindicated.

Then show the cliff: between $b = 0.06$ and $b = 0.08$ four of the five
verdicts flip together. These are not independent detectors. They are one
residual read at different thresholds.

**ASK THE CLASS**
If four tests flip together, what have you learned by running all four?
:::

## Diagnosis, not verdict

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.3 · Thermodynamic consistency testing
:::

::: {.lede}
A failure is the beginning of an investigation. Each fault has a signature.
:::

:::: {.evidence}
| | |
|---|---|
| Constant offset in $\delta y$ | Vapour sampling bias — partial condensation, or a GC calibration offset |
| Residual bowed, one sign throughout | Wrong Antoine constants, or the vapour-phase correction omitted when it mattered |
| Sign change near the azeotrope | Composition analysis non-linear across the range |
| Fails at one end only | Impurity concentrating in the volatile or the heavy component |
| Large ${\rm rms}\,\delta P$ as well | The model, not the data. Refit with a more flexible $G^E$ before concluding anything |
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
This table is the useful output of consistency testing and the part textbooks
omit. Assign it as an exercise: corrupt a good dataset three ways and tabulate
the signatures.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That failing means the paper is wrong. It may mean *your* reduction is wrong —
your Antoine constants, your vapour assumption, your model.
:::

## Building a model from data {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
PART IV
:::

::: {.lede}
Section 4.4&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Regression converges to something for almost any input.<br>The question is never whether a fit exists. It is what the fit is worth.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Open with the hazard: students will believe the first parameter set they
obtain, because it came out of a computer and it plotted nicely. Everything in
this section is a defence against that.
:::

## The objective function is a modelling decision

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.4 · Building an activity coefficient model from data
:::

::: {.lede}
Same data, same model, four objectives, four answers. This is not numerical
noise; it is a choice about which measurement you trust.
:::

![](figures/f4_06_objective_functions.png){.fig-cap width="80%"}

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[The spread is not small]{.card-h .c-rust}

Across objectives the parameters move by several times the standard error that
any one of them reports. An uncertainty that ignores the choice of objective is
understating the real one.

:::

::: {.card}

[Minimise what you measured well]{.card-h .c-teal}

Fitting $\ln\gamma$ weights the dilute ends heavily — precisely where the
measurement is worst. Fitting $y$ fits the least accurate variable. Fitting
$P$ uses the best one.

:::
::::

::: {.source}
F4.6 · Parameters and predictions from three objective functions on one dataset.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Ask them to predict which objective will be worst before showing the numbers.
Most guess $P$, on the grounds that $y$ is "the answer".

**ASK THE CLASS**
Your composition analysis is excellent and your pressure transducer is old.
Does the recommendation change?
:::

## Barker's method

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.4 · Building an activity coefficient model from data
:::

::: {.lede}
Fit to $P$-$x$ alone. Do not fit $y$ at all.
:::

$$P^{\rm calc}(x_1) = x_1 \gamma_1 P_1^{\rm sat} + x_2 \gamma_2 P_2^{\rm sat},
\qquad
\min_{\boldsymbol\theta} \sum_k \left(P^{\rm calc}_k - P^{\rm exp}_k\right)^2$$

:::::: {.cards .g3}
::: {.card}

[It uses the best data]{.card-h .c-teal}

$P$ and $x$ are the two accurately measured variables. Nothing in the objective
depends on the vapour sample.

:::

::: {.card}

[It makes the tests possible]{.card-h .c-amber}

A $y$ that was never fitted can be compared with a $y$ that was measured. That
comparison is the point test and the direct test. Fit $y$ and you destroy your
own diagnostic.

:::

::: {.card}

[Many datasets have no $y$]{.card-h .c-rust}

Static-cell measurements report $P$-$x$ only, by design. Barker is not a
compromise for those data — it is the intended method.

:::
::::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
This is the slide that ties Sections 4.3 and 4.4 together. The consistency
tests are not a separate activity bolted on before fitting; they are what
Barker's method makes available.
:::

## Does the parameter earn its place?

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.4 · Building an activity coefficient model from data
:::

::: {.lede}
A model with more parameters cannot fit worse. The residual alone will always
choose the larger model.
:::

$${\rm AIC} = n \ln\frac{\rm SSE}{n} + 2k$$

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[What AIC answers]{.card-h .c-teal}

Whether the improvement in fit is worth the parameter. A difference below about
2 is conventionally no evidence at all — the data cannot separate those models.

:::

::: {.card}

[Typical outcome]{.card-h .c-amber}

On twenty-one points at realistic noise, Margules, van Laar, Wilson, NRTL and
UNIQUAC land within 2 AIC units of one another. Any claim that one "describes
the system better" needs more than that dataset.

:::
::::

::: {.note}
AIC compares models fitted the same way. It does **not** compare objective
functions: each minimises a different residual vector, so the likelihood being
approximated is not the same likelihood.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Make them state, in one sentence, which model their data actually support. The
honest sentence is usually "the data do not distinguish these four", and
students find that unsatisfying until they see slide F4.8.
:::

## Parameter uncertainty is a region, not two numbers

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.4 · Building an activity coefficient model from data
:::

::: {.lede}
Two standard errors quoted separately describe a rectangle the fit never
occupied.
:::

![](figures/f4_07_bootstrap_confidence_region.png){.fig-cap width="60%"}

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[What the cloud shows]{.card-h .c-rust}

A correlation near $-1$: a long narrow ridge of parameter pairs that fit
equally well. The two parameters are not separately identifiable from one
isotherm.

:::

::: {.card}

[Why bootstrap]{.card-h .c-teal}

The linearised errors assume a quadratic optimum and normal residuals. For two
parameters and twenty points, neither holds well. Resampling makes no such
assumption and is transparent enough to explain in a report.

:::
::::

::: {.source}
F4.7 · Bootstrap replicates with the linearised ellipse over them.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Draw the rectangle implied by two independent error bars on the board, then put
the cloud inside it. The area difference is the argument.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That a strong correlation means the fit is bad. It means the *parameterisation*
is redundant for this experiment. The predictions can still be excellent.
:::

## The consequence that actually matters

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.4 · Building an activity coefficient model from data
:::

::: {.lede}
Two fits the data cannot separate can disagree completely about the region you
care about.
:::

![](figures/f4_08_indistinguishable_fits_lle.png){.fig-cap width="80%"}

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[Same evidence, different claims]{.card-h .c-rust}

Fitted only where data exist, several models agree to within the scatter. They
then report $\gamma^\infty$ differing by tens of per cent, and they do not agree
on whether the liquid splits into two phases.

:::

::: {.card}

[Wilson is the clearest case]{.card-h .c-amber}

Wilson is structurally incapable of predicting a miscibility gap for **any**
parameters. Fitted to a system that has one, it buys the same fit with an
absurd $\gamma^\infty$ instead. That number is a symptom of the functional
form, not a property of the fluid.

:::
::::

::: {.source}
F4.8 · Statistically indistinguishable fits extrapolated beyond the data.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
This is the single most important slide in the module. A liquid-liquid split
predicted outside the data range is a warning about extrapolation, not a
discovery.

**ASK THE CLASS**
You must size a stripper operating at $x_1 = 0.02$ and the data start at 0.55.
Which $\gamma^\infty$ do you use, and what measurement do you ask for first?
:::

## Two ways to find out whether you have learned the noise

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.4 · Building an activity coefficient model from data
:::

::: {.lede}
Reporting the residual on the points you fitted is not evidence.
:::

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[Cross-validation by composition]{.card-h .c-teal}

Train on the middle of the range and predict the dilute ends, then the reverse.
Report both. A model that fits its training points three times better than it
predicts the held-out ones has learned the scatter.

Splitting on alternate points tests almost nothing — neighbouring points carry
almost the same information.

:::

::: {.card}

[Against a prediction]{.card-h .c-amber}

UNIFAC predicts $\gamma$ from group contributions with nothing fitted to your
data. Your model must beat it — it saw the answer. The question is by how much,
and whether the margin survives outside the fitted range.

State the margin in a quantity someone would act on: $\gamma^\infty$, or the
azeotrope composition. Not in rms.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
The UNIFAC comparison is the reality check on the whole enterprise. If two
fitted parameters buy 20 % on $\gamma^\infty$ over a zero-parameter prediction,
say so, and say whether that was worth the experiment.

**ASK THE CLASS**
When would you use UNIFAC in preference to your own fitted parameters?
:::

## Temperature, and the limits of two numbers

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.4 · Building an activity coefficient model from data
:::

::: {.lede}
Parameters fitted at one temperature, used at another.
:::

$$\tau_{ij} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{\Delta u_{ij}}{RT}\right)
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{\partial (G^E/RT)}{\partial T}\Big|_{x} = -\frac{H^E}{RT^2}$$

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[What the extrapolation assumes]{.card-h .c-rust}

Fitting $\tau$ directly at one temperature and reusing it assumes $G^E/RT$ is
independent of $T$ — that is, $H^E = 0$. Fitting $\Delta u$ instead assumes
$\Delta u$ is constant, which is weaker but still an assumption.

:::

::: {.card}

[In practice]{.card-h .c-teal}

Twenty or thirty kelvin is usually tolerable for a non-associating mixture.
Across an alcohol/water column from reboiler to condenser it is not, and the
error shows up exactly where the column is hardest to control.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Tie this back to F4.9: the same $H^E$ that we could not obtain for the isobaric
consistency test is the quantity that governs temperature extrapolation. The
gap in the data appears twice.
:::

## The deliverable

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.4 · Building an activity coefficient model from data
:::

::: {.lede}
A regression report that stops at the parameters is not finished.
:::

:::: {.numbered .n4}
1. **Model, parameters and objective.** Which $G^E$ form, which two numbers, minimised against what, with which vapour-phase assumption.
2. **Range of validity.** The composition, temperature and pressure range of the data, stated as a range and not as a midpoint.
3. **Uncertainty and correlation.** A confidence region or a covariance, not two independent error bars.
4. **What was extrapolated.** Every quantity you report that lies outside the data — $\gamma^\infty$, an azeotrope, a predicted phase split — named as an extrapolation.
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
This list is the marking scheme for the capstone. Say so. Students write the
statement when they know it is marked and not otherwise.

**COMMON MISCONCEPTION**
That the domain of validity is a formality. It is the difference between a
number and an engineering result.
:::

## Using the model {.dark .divider .c-teal background-color="#1C242B"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
PART V
:::

::: {.lede}
Section 4.5&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Bubble, dew, flash — and the question none of them asks.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Short closing section. Its purpose is to connect the fitted model to the
calculations the students will actually run, and to open the door to Module 5.
:::

## Four algorithms, not one

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.5 · Bubble, dew, flash and mixing rules
:::

::: {.lede}
The same equilibrium condition with different variables specified. They do not
converge equally well.
:::

:::::: {.cards .quad}
::: {.card}

[Bubble $P$]{.card-h .c-teal}

Given $x$, $T$. Direct: $\gamma_i(x,T)$ is known immediately, so $P$ and $y$
follow with no iteration for an ideal vapour.

:::

::: {.card}

[Bubble $T$]{.card-h .c-amber}

Given $x$, $P$. One outer iteration on $T$, because $P_i^{\rm sat}$ and
$\gamma_i$ both move with it.

:::

::: {.card}

[Dew $P$]{.card-h .c-rust}

Given $y$, $T$. The liquid composition is unknown, so $\gamma_i$ must be
updated every iteration. Slower and less robust than bubble.

:::

::: {.card}

[Dew $T$]{.card-h .c-sky}

Given $y$, $P$. Both loops at once. This is the one that fails in a flowsheet
at three in the morning.

:::
::::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
The asymmetry between bubble and dew is not incidental, and it is why
simulators do not treat them as one routine. Ask why the unknown being in the
liquid makes the problem harder.
:::

## Rachford-Rice

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.5 · Bubble, dew, flash and mixing rules
:::

::: {.lede}
Monotonic in the vapour fraction, and therefore safe. Show the plot before the
algebra.
:::

$$F(V) = \sum_i \frac{z_i (K_i - 1)}{1 + V(K_i - 1)} = 0,
\qquad K_i = \frac{y_i}{x_i} = \frac{\gamma_i P_i^{\rm sat}}{P}$$

![](figures/f4_10_rachford_rice.png){.fig-lg width="66%"}

::: {.source}
F4.10 · One feed at three pressures. The signs of $F(0)$ and $F(1)$ settle the phase state before any iteration begins.
:::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
${\rm d}F/{\rm d}V < 0$ everywhere, so there is at most one root and bisection
cannot fail. That is the whole reason this formulation is used rather than the
algebraically equivalent ones.

**ASK THE CLASS**
$F(0) < 0$. What have you learned without solving anything?
:::

## The question the flash never asks

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.5 · Bubble, dew, flash and mixing rules
:::

::: {.lede}
Rachford-Rice was told there are two phases, and it will find two phases.
:::

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[What is missing]{.card-h .c-rust}

Nothing in the equilibrium equations checks **how many** phases there should
be. A fitted model that predicts a liquid-liquid split will still return a
single perfectly reasonable-looking liquid composition inside the gap.

:::

::: {.card}

[What answers it]{.card-h .c-teal}

The Gibbs energy of mixing and a tangent construction — not the equilibrium
equations. A liquid splits when $\Delta g_{\rm mix}$ dips below its own chord.
That is Module 5, and it is why the capstone spans both modules.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Demonstrate the failure rather than describing it: flash a feed inside the
predicted miscibility gap and show the plausible wrong answer. Then show the
$\Delta g_{\rm mix}$ curve.
:::

## Mixing rules for cubic equations of state

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.5 · Bubble, dew, flash and mixing rules
:::

::: {.lede}
The phi-phi route needs mixture parameters. The classical answer is quadratic
in composition.
:::

$$a_{\rm mix} = \sum_i\sum_j x_i x_j \sqrt{a_i a_j}\,(1 - k_{ij}),
\qquad b_{\rm mix} = \sum_i x_i b_i$$

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[$k_{ij}$ is fitted, not predicted]{.card-h .c-amber}

It comes from binary data, exactly like the activity model parameters, and it
carries the same obligations: a range of validity and an uncertainty.

:::

::: {.card}

[Why it fails for polar mixtures]{.card-h .c-rust}

The quadratic form assumes random mixing. Substituting it into the cubic gives
an excess Gibbs energy that is thermodynamically equivalent to a one-constant
Margules model: symmetric, one parameter. Hydrogen-bonding mixtures are neither
symmetric nor one-parameter, and $k_{ij}$ can scale that curve but cannot change
its shape.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
The Margules equivalence is the sharpest way to state the failure. It is not
that the rule is inaccurate; it is that it has the wrong functional form and no
value of $k_{ij}$ can repair it.
:::

## One idea, stated and not derived

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
4.5 · Bubble, dew, flash and mixing rules
:::

::: {.lede}
A mixing rule can be constructed so that a cubic equation of state reproduces a
chosen excess Gibbs energy model.
:::

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[What that buys]{.card-h .c-teal}

The pressure range and the supercritical components of an equation of state,
together with the composition behaviour of NRTL or UNIQUAC. This is how a
simulator handles CO₂ with ethanol at 100 bar.

:::

::: {.card}

[Where to find it]{.card-h .c-amber}

Huron-Vidal and Wong-Sandler. Four appendix slides follow this one, and the
algebra is in **`vle-mixing-rules-note.pdf`** on the course page. Not lectured,
not examined — but the property-method dropdown in a simulator says PRWS and
PSRK, and four pages is what it takes to know what that means.

:::
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Say explicitly that this is not examinable and that it matters to the students
who go on to high-pressure or polar systems. Naming who it is for is what stops
the rest of the class worrying about it.
:::

## What you must be able to do

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Closing
:::

::: {.lede}
The module in six statements.
:::

:::: {.numbered .n3 .two-col}
1. **Choose a description and defend the assumption.** Raoult, modified Raoult, gamma-phi or phi-phi — and say which assumption you are relying on.
2. **Turn $T$, $P$, $x$, $y$ into $\gamma$ with its uncertainty.** Including the vapour-phase assumption, stated, and the error in $P^{\rm sat}$.
3. **Test a dataset and diagnose the failure.** All five tests, and a signature-based diagnosis rather than a verdict.
4. **Fit, and say what the fit is worth.** Objective chosen deliberately, confidence region reported, extrapolations named.
5. **Compare against a prediction.** Know what the two fitted parameters bought over UNIFAC.
6. **Know what the calculation does not check.** A flash assumes the number of phases. Module 5 supplies the missing test.
::::

::: {.notes}
**TEACHING TIP**
Return to the opening statement: a parameter set is not a result. Ask whether
anyone would now use a published NRTL pair without checking the paper's
consistency table and composition range.
:::

## &nbsp; {.dark .mid background-color="#1C242B" visibility="uncounted"}

:::: {.vcenter}
::: {.statement}
Appendix
:::

::: {.statement-hi}
EoS-$G^E$ mixing rules<br>Huron-Vidal and Wong-Sandler
:::

::: {.statement-sub}
Not lectured. Not examined. Read the note if this is your problem.
:::
::::

## A.1 · Two worlds that do not meet {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Appendix · EoS-$G^E$ mixing rules
:::

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[Equations of state]{.card-h .c-teal}

Handle high pressure and supercritical components. One model for both phases,
no reference vapour pressure required. Fail on polar and hydrogen-bonding
mixtures, because the quadratic mixing rule assumes random mixing.

:::

::: {.card}

[Activity coefficient models]{.card-h .c-rust}

Handle polar and associating liquids, through local-composition terms fitted to
data. Cannot cross the critical point, and need a reference fugacity that a
supercritical component does not have.

:::
::::

::: {.note}
The engineering problem is the mixture that is both — CO₂ with ethanol, water
with a light gas — and neither description can be pushed into the other's
territory. The mixing rule is the bridge.
:::

## A.2 · Huron-Vidal {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Appendix · EoS-$G^E$ mixing rules
:::

::: {.lede}
Match the excess Gibbs energy of the equation of state to that of an activity
model in the infinite-pressure limit, where the cubic collapses to $V = b$ and
the expression closes.
:::

$$\frac{a_{\rm mix}}{b_{\rm mix}}
 = \sum_i x_i \frac{a_i}{b_i} - \frac{g^E_\infty}{C},
\qquad
C = \frac{1}{\delta_1 - \delta_2}\,\ln\frac{1 + \delta_1}{1 + \delta_2}$$

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[The constant]{.card-h .c-teal}

$C = \ln 2 = 0.6931$ for Soave-Redlich-Kwong;
$C = \ln(1+\sqrt2)/\sqrt2 = 0.6232$ for Peng-Robinson.

:::

::: {.card}

[The practical cost]{.card-h .c-rust}

**Published low-pressure NRTL parameters cannot be reused.** The reference
state is the infinite-pressure limit, not the real liquid, so the parameters
must be refitted — and they are not transferable between SRK and PR either,
because $C$ differs.

:::
::::

## A.3 · Wong-Sandler {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Appendix · EoS-$G^E$ mixing rules
:::

::: {.lede}
Keep the infinite-pressure condition and add the low-density one: the second
virial coefficient must be quadratic in composition.
:::

$$B = b - \frac{a}{RT},
\qquad
Q = \sum_i\sum_j x_i x_j B_{ij},
\qquad
D = \sum_i x_i \frac{a_i}{b_i RT} + \frac{g^E_\infty}{CRT}$$

$$b_{\rm mix} = \frac{Q}{1 - D},
\qquad
a_{\rm mix} = RT\,\frac{Q\,D}{1 - D}$$

:::: {.cards}
::: {.card}

[What is gained]{.card-h .c-teal}

Correct at both ends of the density range. $b_{\rm mix}$ stops being linear in
composition, which is the structural difference from Huron-Vidal.

:::

::: {.card}

[What it costs]{.card-h .c-amber}

One extra binary parameter in the $B_{ij}$ combining rule, on top of the $g^E$
model parameters. Pure-component reduction ($b_{\rm mix} = b_i$,
$a_{\rm mix} = a_i$) is the unit test to run before trusting an implementation.

:::
::::

## A.4 · What the names mean {visibility="uncounted"}

::: {.kicker .c-amber}
Appendix · EoS-$G^E$ mixing rules
:::

| Property method | Is | Parameters |
|---|---|---|
| PRWS, RKSWS | Wong-Sandler on PR or SRK | Refit; not the published low-pressure set |
| PRMHV2, RKSMHV2 | Modified Huron-Vidal, second order | Zero-pressure reference — published UNIFAC/UNIQUAC parameters **can** be reused |
| PSRK | Predictive SRK: MHV1 with UNIFAC | Predictive; no binary VLE data needed |

::: {.note}
MHV1 and MHV2 (Michelsen, 1990) use a zero-pressure rather than an
infinite-pressure reference, which is precisely what makes published parameters
transferable. That is their entire practical advantage.
:::

::: {.source}
Full derivations, the sign-convention warning, and the references: `vle-mixing-rules-note.pdf`.
:::
